items.body_md:
Today's docket is narrower than yesterday's — no rulings, no adversary filings — but the claim-transfer activity at Dkts. 1164 and 1165 (both filed August 7) extends the secondary-market repositioning pattern that opened August 6 with Dkts. 1158 and 1159. Four claim assignments have now been processed through claims agent Epiq Corporate Restructuring, LLC across a 48-hour window immediately following 
plan confirmation, which Harvest Sherwood received at the August 5 hearing after Judge Jernigan overruled the remaining U.S. Trustee objection
 (__[Law360](https://www.law360.com/articles/2510100/harvest-sherwood-wins-ch-11-plan-approval)__). That clustering is not incidental: a now-confirmed plan provides the price-discovery anchor that secondary-market buyers need to underwrite claim acquisitions, and the volume here suggests at least two distinct purchasers are building or topping up positions in quick succession. Each transfer of record under Bankruptcy Rule 3001(e)(2) carries a 21-day notice period before the transferee can be substituted as holder; claimants monitoring their own claims should confirm whether any transfer notice implicates their position.

The compensation filing at Dkt. 1157 (August 6) — the day's only substantive administrative entry beyond the claim transfers and the pro hac vice admissions covered yesterday — continues the professional-fee cadence running parallel to McDermott Will & Schulte LLP's thirteenth monthly fee statement at Dkt. 1143 for the June 1 through June 30, 2026 period. The identity of the applicant at Dkt. 1157 is not yet confirmed from publicly available sources; the filing's recovery-posture relevance depends on whether it reflects estate professionals, plan-funder counsel, or a new entrant, and that question is worth tracking when the order comes through. The certificate at Dkt. 1163 (August 6) has no immediate strategic implication. Nothing filed today or yesterday alters the relief from stay motion at Dkt. 1162, which remains the most tactically interesting open item from August 6 — a creditor moving against collateral or a co-obligor with the plan framework now settled, but whose target and claim size are not yet publicly confirmed.

The next hard deadline with direct recovery consequence remains the adversary trial in *Harvest Sherwood v. Sprouts Farmers Market*, Adv. Pro. 25-08002, before Judge Jernigan on September 21, 2026, alongside 
Atlas Grove Management's position as plan funder, pursuing more than $1 billion in antitrust litigation claims against more than 25 defendants primarily across the chicken, pork, and beef producer industries
 (__[ABF Journal](https://www.abfjournal.com/atlas-grove-gains-court-approval-for-180mm-financing-commitment-for-harvest-sherwood-bankruptcy-estate/)__). Between now and September 21, the principal monitoring items are: the entry of the formal confirmation order (not yet docketed as a signed order in today's run), satisfaction of any conditions to plan effectiveness, and further claim-transfer filings that will continue to signal secondary-market conviction on the recovery quantum.

items.body_md:
Today's docket movement is narrow but structurally legible: five entries filed August 7 — Dkt. 68 through Dkt. 72 — consist entirely of pro hac vice motions (Dkt. 69, 70) and their corresponding orders granting admission (Dkt. 71, 72), plus a notice of appearance (Dkt. 68) and an attorney-addition event. The filings do not identify the admitting attorneys or the parties they represent on the face of the ground truth provided, and those particulars are unverified; what is clear is that at least two new attorneys obtained leave to appear in the case today under D. Del. LR 9010-1. That pattern — a cluster of pro hac vice admissions arriving together — is typically a signal that a new constituency is organizing its representation, whether a significant creditor, a potential bidder, or a party with a stake in the governance dispute. Until the underlying motions are reviewed for the identity of counsel and client, the implications for the recovery posture remain uncertain, though the timing is notable: this activity arrives eleven days before the August 19 objection deadline for the first-day operational orders and twenty-seven days before the September 3 final hearing before Judge Karen Owens.

Dkt. 67, the Stretto affidavit of service filed August 5 and reported in yesterday's briefing, has since drawn regional press attention confirming the same headline figures already in the record. The Herald-Dispatch's August 5 report restates the governance contest between CEO Hindman's management team and the Gassheimer/Omnis Energy faction, and notes that 
the $50.9 million unsecured loan obligation to the West Virginia Economic Development Authority arises from a 2023 loan to Quantum Pleasants LLC to support the not-achieved conversion of the Pleasants Power Station into a hydrogen production facility.
 That framing matters to the WVEDA's recovery posture: the obligation sits unsecured, no committee has been formed to represent the general unsecured class (Dkt. 66), and the governance dispute — which turns on whether Gassheimer's appointment as interim director after 
Quantum Pleasants as sole equity owner removed Nathan as independent manager on July 20
 is valid — remains unresolved on the Delaware docket. The Herald-Dispatch coverage adds no new primary-source filings beyond what was covered yesterday, but its publication confirms the story is receiving sustained West Virginia press attention, which may accelerate pressure on the U.S. Trustee to convene a creditors' committee. __[Herald-Dispatch](https://www.herald-dispatch.com/news/omnis-pleasants-reports-600-creditors-70-in-wv-amid-uncertain-coal-plant-future/article_5b21adc9-1c75-433a-be51-5ed26f74a819.html)__

The next concrete milestone remains August 19, 2026 — the objection deadline for the first-day operational orders set by Dkt. 57 — followed by the September 3 final hearing at 824 Market Street, Courtroom 3, Wilmington, at 1:00 PM. The identities of the parties newly entering appearances today should be treated as a priority item to confirm from the underlying motion papers; if today's pro hac vice admissions represent a significant creditor or adverse party organizing into the governance dispute, the complexion of the August 19 objection period could shift materially.

items.body_md:
Today's objection deadline has now closed — or closes by end of business — and the docket has delivered its most significant procedural development since the support cluster filed August 6: Dkt. 98, filed this morning, is logged as an Objection, the first contested filing against the bidding procedures and sale motion in *In re Poolin Technology PTE*, No. 26-18325 (Bankr. D.N.J., Judge O'Hagan). The identity of the objecting party and the precise grounds are not confirmed from docket text available to this briefing, but the filing's timing — the deadline itself — is consistent with a creditor, committee, or regulatory body preserving its objection rights for the August 14 hearing. Whether this is a targeted objection to a specific bid term, a broader challenge to the § 363 framework, or a cure-related filing cannot be stated with certainty at this stage; that content governs how the August 14 hearing is shaped and whether Judge O'Hagan proceeds, adjourns, or takes the matter on a contested basis.

Also filed this morning is Dkt. 97, logged as a Meeting of Creditors Chapter 11. 
Objections to the bidding procedures and sale motion were due August 7, and the court has scheduled a hearing for August 14 at 11 a.m. ET.
 The § 341 meeting entry is procedurally routine but confirms the case is tracking standard Chapter 11 administration in parallel with the sale process — it does not bear directly on recovery posture unless an examiner or U.S. Trustee observation surfaces anything adverse at that session. The undocketed Notice of Docketing Error, also filed August 7, has no confirmed substantive effect; such notices typically correct a filing deficiency rather than alter the underlying record. Against this backdrop, the six support filings from August 6 (Dkt. 89–94) now sit alongside a live objection: the procedural picture heading into August 14 is contested, not clean.

The objection's existence sharpens the stakes of the two concurrent pressures already in play. 
Thor may terminate through August 9 if, in its sole and absolute discretion, it finds diligence unsatisfactory, for any reason or no reason, leaving a no-cause exit three days before the requested bid-procedures hearing.
 A stalking-horse termination arriving simultaneously with a contested objection hearing would present Judge O'Hagan with a materially weakened sale framework: no floor bid, no approved procedures, and a contested § 363 record. 
Neither purchase agreement fixes how consideration divides between the two Lonestar estates — each leaves allocation to the buyer to be determined within 180 days after closing — and Poolin Technology is not a seller under either agreement.
 For the 11,700 wallet holders carrying $163,723,500 in unsecured IOU claims, that structural gap remains the central unresolved variable; 
the amount available to wallet creditors depends on estate-specific claims, any valid liens against net proceeds, transfer taxes, professional fees, other administrative costs, and the treatment of Poolin's intercompany claim.
 The next two milestones arrive in sequence: Thor's no-cause diligence exit right expires August 9, and the bid-procedures and sale hearing before Judge O'Hagan follows on August 14 at 11 a.m. ET — now against a docket that carries at least one live objection.

items.body_md:
The press coverage that landed August 5–6 fills in the structural detail on Anthropic's Concord II partial dismissal motions that yesterday's edition flagged at the level of their existence and general thrust. The more precise picture, now confirmed across multiple sources, is that Anthropic is not seeking to dismiss the core torrenting and training allegations — those remain live — but is instead targeting two specific, downstream claims: the output-based infringement count, and a Digital Millennium Copyright Act count. 
Anthropic argued that the complaint, covering roughly 21,000 works, never cites one instance of Claude reproducing a lyric, and asked that the output claim be dismissed with prejudice.
 The "with prejudice" ask is the sharpest edge here: if granted, the publishers would be barred from replying that claim in its current form, eliminating what would otherwise be the most direct mechanism to show consumer-facing harm at trial. 
Anthropic also moved to dismiss the DMCA count, arguing the statute reaches only the stripping of copyright management information from a complete work, and that the publishers never allege Anthropic held their full compositions.
 That DMCA theory, if it had survived, would have provided a separate damages floor independent of statutory copyright damages — its loss narrows the publishers' damages architecture in Concord II, though it has no direct bearing on the infringement claims already advancing in 5:24-cv-03811. 
The two filings landed on Monday, August 3, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California.



Concord II carries case number 5:26-cv-00880, was filed January 28, 2026, and names Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and co-founder Benjamin Mann as individual defendants
 — the confirmed case number is worth logging cleanly given the parallel docket management now running alongside 5:24-cv-03811. 
Amodei filed separately to get the direct infringement count against him personally dropped; Anthropic did not move against the torrenting and training claims, which it continues to contest.
 The strategic implication for rights-holders in both proceedings is that Anthropic has chosen to fight the input-side allegations on the merits while attempting to clear the output-side and DMCA theories at the pleading stage — a posture that, if successful, would concentrate the entire evidentiary burden of the litigation on the training-data conduct and away from anything Claude does in response to user prompts. Whether the publishers can amend to supply the missing output examples, or whether the court grants dismissal with prejudice on that count, will materially affect the damages ceiling they can present to any jury in Concord II.

Nothing new has landed on the Concord I docket (5:24-cv-03811) since yesterday's edition. The next concrete event remains the Case Management Conference before Judge Lee on Zoom on September 2, 2026, followed by the Summary Judgment Hearing on October 21, 2026 — at which the fair use and direct infringement questions in the original case will be the focus. The Concord II partial dismissal argument on November 4 then follows, meaning Judge Lee will have issued her summary judgment ruling in Concord I, or will be close to doing so, at the point she hears the threshold pleading challenges in Concord II. That sequencing matters: a summary judgment ruling adverse to Anthropic on training-data fair use in Concord I would substantially undercut the legal premise of the same argument Anthropic is mounting in Concord II.

items.body_md:
The most consequential entry since yesterday's briefing is Dkt. 145, filed August 6: an Emergency Motion whose subject matter is not specified in the ground truth but whose procedural posture demands attention. Emergency motions in large Chapter 11 cases are typically filed under Bankruptcy Local Rule 9013 when a matter cannot wait for the next scheduled hearing — here, the second-day hearing set for August 24 in Bankr. S.D. Tex., Case No. 26-90737, before Judge Lopez. The nature of the relief sought is not yet confirmed from the docket entry alone, and the committee formed the same day under Dkt. 137 will have standing to weigh in; its counsel should be pulling that filing immediately. Whatever the subject, the motion's emergency designation means Judge Lopez will likely set an expedited briefing and hearing schedule that compresses the August 24 timeline or creates an intervening hearing date — a development creditors should track for objection deadlines that may ripen before the second-day hearing.

Alongside the emergency motion, Dkt. 144 carries a Statement filed August 6, the nature of which is also unspecified in the ground truth. In context — filed the same day the U.S. Trustee published the committee appointment notice and one day after PBGC filed dual appearances — the statement is most plausibly a party-in-interest disclosure or position statement staking out a creditor's or the U.S. Trustee's posture on a contested matter. It warrants a direct pull to confirm the filer and substance. The continued accumulation of pro hac vice admissions (Dkts. 139 and 141) reinforces the picture of a case where the adversarial bench is now fully assembling: each new admission corresponds to an out-of-district attorney joining a party with a substantive, not merely monitoring, role. 
RNDC carries roughly US$400 million in obligations to unsecured creditors, many of whom are smaller suppliers that face material financial difficulty of their own if recoveries fall short
 — the depth of creditor engagement the docket reflects is proportionate to that exposure.

On the transactional side, the nunc pro tunc motion at Dkt. 123 — the debtors' request for retroactive authority over RNDC New York, LLC's sale and related restrictive covenants — remains unresolved and is almost certain to be folded into the August 24 second-day agenda. The newly constituted Official Committee of Unsecured Creditors (Dkt. 137) now has estate funding and full 11 U.S.C. § 1102 standing to investigate that transaction, and its first concrete leverage point remains conditioning non-objection on disclosure of the full economics of the New York disposition. 
Court filings indicate the debtors made more than US$700 million in tax distributions to direct equityholders
 — __[New Chapter 11 Bankruptcy Filing – Republic National Distributing Company LLC](https://www.petition11.com/p/rndc-chapter-11-bankruptcy-filing)__ — a figure the committee's professionals will weigh against the prepetition asset sale proceeds as they map the scope of any avoidance or clawback analysis. The schedules of assets and liabilities and statements of financial affairs remain due September 23, 2026, the 59-day extension deadline; those filings will be the first comprehensive on-record accounting of estate assets and intercompany flows, and they will anchor both the committee's investigation and the adequacy analysis of the joint disclosure statement filed at Dkt. 118. The next hard deadline is August 24 (Bankr. S.D. Tex., Case No. 26-90737, Judge Lopez, 1:00 p.m. CT): the second-day hearing at which the committee will make its first public appearance, interim orders are expected to convert to final, and the emergency motion at Dkt. 145 — if not resolved on an expedited basis before that date — will be on the table.

items.body_md:
*In re Sleep Number Corporation, et al.*, Case No. 26-11399 (KYP), U.S. Bankruptcy Court, S.D.N.Y. (Hon. Kyu Young Paek). Today's delta is modest in volume but not in significance: the single most consequential filing from the August 6 cluster — Dkt. 526, the Second Stipulation With Prepetition Loan Agent Extending Committee Challenge Deadline Pursuant To Final DIP Financing Order — was flagged in yesterday's briefing as unverified and remains so from available public sources. Its substance now warrants direct attention. Under a standard final DIP order, the Official Committee of Unsecured Creditors receives a defined window to investigate and, if warranted, challenge the validity, priority, or extent of prepetition secured liens — here, the liens securing the $260 million DIP facility documented as the Fourteenth Amendment to the existing Amended and Restated Credit and Security Agreement, with U.S. Bank National Association as administrative agent (__[Bondoro](https://bondoro.com/sleep-number/)__). A second stipulation extending that deadline, agreed between the Committee and the prepetition loan agent, signals that the investigation is live and that the Committee has not yet exhausted its review — or has identified issues that require more time to develop. For unsecured creditors, any successful challenge to lien validity or scope is the clearest path to enlarging the unencumbered asset pool available for general distribution; each extension of the challenge deadline preserves that optionality. The specific new deadline set by Dkt. 526 is not summarized in available public sources and should be confirmed against the docket directly.

The Third Designation Rights Period Rejection Notice (Dkt. 525) and the related A&G Realty Partners retention order (Dkt. 522) were covered yesterday; no new public reporting has moved on either entry since. The Deloitte & Touche LLP independent auditor application (Dkt. 520, effective July 14, 2026) similarly requires no additional treatment today — it is an administrative professional-retention filing, not a dispositive creditor event — though its July 14 effective date, nearly three weeks after the petition date of June 12, 2026, is worth noting as a data point on the pace at which post-sale audit infrastructure is being assembled. 
The § 341 meeting of creditors was held by Zoom conference on July 24, 2026
, and the estate is now deep in the post-sale administrative phase; professional retention and fee disclosure filings will continue to accumulate through the bar date period. The fee statements filed August 5 — Davis Polk's first monthly statement at Dkt. 516 and Vinson & Elkins' first monthly statement at Dkt. 517, both covering June 12 through June 30, 2026 — remain without publicly summarized dollar figures. Creditors focused on administrative expense accrual should pull both filings directly; the Special Investigation Committee's Vinson & Elkins engagement in particular bears watching as fee statements accumulate, since the pace of billing reflects the pace of the underlying potential-claims review.

The next concrete milestones are August 20, 2026 (adjourned case conference at 10:00 a.m. in Courtroom 610, New York, at which the Third Designation Rights Period Rejection Notice objection deadline also falls), and 
September 10, 2026 at 11:59 p.m. (ET), the General Claims Bar Date
 — now 34 days out. Any creditor that has not yet filed a proof of claim should treat August 20 as the practical last-review date before the bar date window closes.

items.body_md:
The docket moved modestly in the 48-hour window since yesterday's edition. Three filings landed on August 6 — Dkt. 557 (Certificate of No Objection — No Order Required) and Dkts. 558 and 559 (Certificates of Service) — with a fourth Certificate of Service having been filed on August 5 as Dkt. 556. The Certificate of No Objection at Dkt. 557 is the substantive marker: under the standard Delaware fee-application protocol, a certificate of no objection filed without an accompanying proposed order signals that the underlying relief — almost certainly a monthly or interim professional compensation request — is deemed granted by the court on a non-contested basis, without a formal hearing. No party filed a response within the objection window, which is the expected cadence at this post-confirmation stage of the case, but it does advance the professional fee consumption clock and narrows the fee reserve available to satisfy creditor distributions.

The broader arc remains unchanged: 
Judge Thomas M. Horan confirmed the Second Amended Joint Chapter 11 Plan at Dkt. 527 on July 13, 2026
, and the Keyrock sale closed contemporaneously. 
The Verita case-administration page reflects a September 11, 2026 (4:00 p.m. ET) deadline
 as the next docketed date of consequence — __[Verita Global (BlockFills case page)](https://www.veritaglobal.net/blockfills)__ — which is consistent with a post-effective-date administrative claims or plan supplement deadline; the precise nature of that deadline is not confirmed in the materials reviewed this morning and should be verified directly against the confirmed plan or the Verita docket. What is clear is that the case has entered its post-confirmation administrative phase, with professional fee processing and service logistics constituting the bulk of near-term docket activity. For claimants, the operative question is how quickly the liquidating trust can resolve claims against the estate's roughly 
$145 million in general unsecured obligations
 — __[chapter11cases.com](https://chapter11cases.com/blogs/news/blockfills-parent-files-chapter-11-in-delaware-proposes-customer-led-reorganization-into-newco)__ — against a recovery pool anchored by the 
court-entered solicitation and distribution procedures order at Dkt. 388
 and the $3.25 million Keyrock sale proceeds. __[Verita Global (BlockFills case page)](https://www.veritaglobal.net/blockfills)__

The next concrete milestone is September 11, 2026 (4:00 p.m. ET), per the Verita case page — __[Verita Global (BlockFills case page)](https://www.veritaglobal.net/blockfills)__ — though claimants should confirm the specific procedural significance of that date directly against the confirmed plan. No contested hearings, adversary proceedings, or substantive dispositive filings are visible on the docket in the current window. The rhythm of service certificates and non-contested fee approvals is normal for this stage and, standing alone, presents no new recovery risk.

Walrath signed Dkt. 39, the Order Granting Provisional Relief Pursuant to 11 U.S.C. § 1519 — putting a U.S. statutory stay in place pending the recognition hearing — and simultaneously entered Dkt. 40, the Order Scheduling the Hearing on Recognition of the Chapter 15 Petition and specifying the form and manner of notice.
items.body_md:
The two most consequential filings of the week both landed on August 5. Judge Mary F. Walrath signed Dkt. 39, the Order Granting Provisional Relief Pursuant to 11 U.S.C. § 1519 — putting a U.S. statutory stay in place pending the recognition hearing — and simultaneously entered Dkt. 40, the Order Scheduling the Hearing on Recognition of the Chapter 15 Petition and specifying the form and manner of notice. Those two orders together convert what was, through Tuesday, a petition supported only by the Tel Aviv District Court's August 2 domestic stay into a proceeding with active U.S. federal protection. 
If the Delaware court grants full recognition, Firy Inc. (formerly Skillz) would be blocked from collecting on the $719 million judgment while Papaya's appeal runs its course.
 The § 1519 provisional order holds that position in the interim. Dkt. 41, filed the same day, is the notice of hearing distributed to parties; Dkt. 42, filed August 5, is the certificate of service confirming that distribution went out.

Yesterday, August 6, the docket absorbed six more practitioner-entry filings — Dkts. 43 through 49 — consisting of one appearance notice and three pro hac vice motions (Dkts. 44–46) paired with three corresponding admission orders (Dkts. 47–49). Four pro hac vice admissions were already entered by order on August 4 (covering Coleman, Raynal, Carpenito, and Davidson per Dkts. 29–32), so the roster of admitted counsel is now materially larger. That volume of new appearances at this early stage suggests parties beyond the debtor and the primary judgment creditor are positioning themselves in the proceeding — the identities of the newly appearing counsel are not confirmed in the materials available, but the pattern is consistent with additional creditors or interested parties establishing standing ahead of the recognition hearing. The recognition hearing date itself was set by Dkt. 40 but is not confirmed in the current docket ground truth; 
the next key threshold question is whether the U.S. Bankruptcy Court will grant Chapter 15 recognition.


For Firy's recovery posture, the operative tension remains unchanged in structure but has now sharpened in timing: provisional § 1519 relief is live, which means collection is stayed, but the recognition order — the mechanism that makes that stay durable — has not yet issued. 
Under the terms presented to the Israeli court, Papaya will transfer available cash balances into a designated fund overseen by a court-appointed official, with that fund expected to hold approximately $100 million during 2026 as a potential source for settling claims should the U.S. ruling become enforceable in Israel.
 
The $719 million disgorgement figure was entered in lieu of the $420 million in actual damages awarded by the jury in April 2026, as Firy is entitled to recover once for its injury.
 The gap between the fund's projected 2026 ceiling and the judgment face value is the central recovery constraint, and the pace at which that fund is populated — and by whom it is overseen — will deserve close attention as the Israeli proceeding develops in parallel. The next concrete milestone in Delaware is the recognition hearing scheduled by Dkt. 40; that date governs when Judge Walrath can enter the order that would make the automatic-stay effect of § 1520 operative against Firy's collection efforts on a permanent rather than provisional basis.

items.body_md:
*In re Terraform Labs Pte. Ltd., Bankr. D. Del., Case No. 24-10070-BLS, Judge Brendan Linehan Shannon*

The only new docket activity since Wednesday's edition is Dkt. 1319, an Objection filed August 5, 2026. The docket entry designation — "Objection" without further qualification in the publicly available record — places it squarely in the pattern that has defined this estate's post-confirmation phase: contested claim allowance, disputed claim transfers, or resistance to a pending motion. The filing lands two days after a cluster of four claim transfers (Dkts. 1309–1312, August 3), the most recent of which assigned a $3,454,036.42 claim from a redacted transferor to Serrur Investment Partners, LP via TerraClaim LLC, signaling continued secondary-market activity in the claims pool. Whether Dkt. 1319 targets one of those transfers, challenges a valuation determination on the crypto loss claims register, or contests some other pending matter cannot be confirmed from publicly available sources as of this briefing; the filing's substance requires PACER access to the full document.

What is clear is the structural context: 
more than two years after Terraform Labs entered chapter 11, its confirmed liquidating plan remains in active administration, and as of the post-confirmation report for the quarter ending March 31, 2026, the Wind Down Trust had distributed nothing to plan creditors, even as the plan administrator continued reconciling more than 16,000 crypto loss claims and pressing a $4 billion lawsuit against Jump Trading as the estate's largest affirmative recovery effort
 (__[Elevenflo](https://elevenflo.com/blog/terraform-labs-bankruptcy)__). An objection at Dkt. 1319 — whatever its precise target — lands in an estate where claim allowance determinations are the direct gating mechanism for eventual distributions. Any successful objection that disallows or reduces a claim expands the recoverable pool for remaining allowed creditors; any objection that fails preserves a competing draw on that pool. The post-confirmation reports filed July 30 (Dkts. 1306–1307) will also repay review once accessible, as they will reflect the trust's asset position for the most recent quarterly period and may reveal whether the cash runway supports the litigation posture in the Jump and Jane Street proceedings.

The next concrete milestone to track is any response deadline or hearing date tied to Dkt. 1319, which under Local Rule 9006-1(c) would typically run 14 days from service absent a separate scheduling order. On the litigation front, the plan administrator's motion to dismiss the Chang adversary proceeding (Adv. Proc. 26-50229) remains pending before Judge Shannon following the July 2026 filing reported last month (__[Law360](https://www.law360.com/bankruptcy-authority/mid-cap/articles/2504885)__), and the Jane Street insider-trading action in the Southern District of New York continues to be contested on the motion-to-dismiss briefing that closed in June (__[Law360](https://www.law360.com/bankruptcy/articles/2489043)__). Neither of those proceedings generated new docket activity in the lookback window.
